headline: Burnham says Britain could campaign to rejoin the EU at the next election

levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he could campaign to take Britain back into the European Union at the next general election, reopening the debate a decade after the 2016 Brexit referendum.
In a BBC interview aired on Wednesday, Burnham set out three options he plans to discuss at a UK-EU summit later this year: rejoining the EU, rejoining the single market, or entering a customs union. Pressed by Nick Robinson, he said he had written in his book that he would like to see Britain rejoin in his lifetime, but added that this did not necessarily mean now.
Burnham stressed he would stick to Labour's current manifesto for the rest of this parliament, which rules out the single market and customs union. He wants to agree a new direction at the summit and then put it to voters at the next election, which he has said will be in 2029.
levels.headline: Burnham says Britain could campaign to rejoin the EU at the next election
levels.why: It is the clearest signal yet from a sitting prime minister that Brexit could be reversed or softened, and it is likely to make Europe a central issue at the 2029 election.

Speaking to Nick Robinson in a BBC interview on Wednesday, he set out three options he wants to discuss with European leaders at a summit later this year. The UK could rejoin the EU fully, rejoin the single market, which lets goods and services trade freely, or join a customs union, which removes import taxes between members.
Burnham admitted he had written in his book that he hoped Britain would rejoin in his lifetime, but said that did not necessarily mean now. Until the next election, which he expects in 2029, he says he will keep Labour's promise to stay outside the single market and customs union.

In a BBC interview, he said he will talk to EU leaders at a meeting later this year about three options. The first is rejoining the EU completely. The second is rejoining its single market, which makes trade easier. The third is a customs union, which removes taxes on goods crossing the border.

Now the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has told the BBC that Britain could think about rejoining. He wants to discuss closer ties with European leaders at a meeting later this year. He said there are three choices: joining the EU again, joining its trading area, called the single market, or joining a customs union, which would stop taxes on goods crossing borders.
Burnham says he won't make these changes before the next general election in 2029. Instead, he wants to explain his ideas and let voters decide then.
levels.headline: Could Britain go back into the EU?

He will meet European leaders later this year to talk about it. One idea is joining the EU again. Another is just making trade with Europe easier again.
He says nothing will change before the next general election in 2029. He wants voters to decide then. That means rejoining Europe could become one of the biggest questions at that election.

headline: Fifteen candidates contest Holborn and St Pancras by-election on 8 October

levels.body:
Voters in the London constituency of Holborn and St Pancras go to the polls on 8 October, with 15 candidates on the ballot. Labour has selected Camden Council leader Sagal Abdi-Wali. Zack Polanski, leader of the Green Party of England and Wales since September 2025 and a London Assembly member since 2021, is standing for the Greens. Former Camden councillor Ewan Cameron represents the Conservatives.
George Galloway is standing for the Workers Party, alongside candidates from Reform UK and the Liberal Democrats and a long list of smaller parties and independents, including the Official Monster Raving Loony Party and the Climate Party. Betting odds on Labour shortened in late September.
The contest comes with Reform UK, led by Nigel Farage, having led national opinion polls since early 2025.

headline: UK 10-year gilt yield holds near 19-year high as rate-rise fears linger

levels.body:
The yield on the UK's benchmark 10-year government bond, known as a gilt, ended September just under 5.4%, slightly below the 19-year high it reached earlier in the month. It stood at 5.38% on 25 September and around 5.40% on 1 October.
Gilt yields rise when investors sell government debt and demand a higher return to lend. The main worries are persistent inflation, which rose to 3.1% in August, and a more hawkish Bank of England, where three of nine policymakers voted for a rate rise in September. A sell-off in US Treasuries, which pushed the US 10-year yield to its highest since 2007, has added to the pressure.
Sterling recovered towards $1.34 against the dollar after touching an almost four-week low.
Higher gilt yields increase the government's debt-interest bill, reducing room for spending or tax cuts. They also feed into the swap rates lenders use to price fixed-rate mortgages.

levels.why: Higher gilt yields raise the government's debt-interest bill, reducing room for spending and tax decisions ahead of the Budget. They also feed through to the swap rates lenders use to price fixed-rate mortgages.

The government borrows money by selling bonds called gilts to investors. The interest it pays depends on how confident those investors feel. At the moment, they are worried that prices are still rising too quickly, and that the Bank of England might have to put interest rates up again. Rising borrowing costs in the US are also having an effect.
The pound steadied at around $1.34.
This matters because the more the government spends on interest, the less it has for public services. It can also push up the cost of fixed-rate mortgages for homeowners.

When the UK government needs money, it borrows it by selling bonds called gilts. In return, it pays interest to the people who buy them.
Right now, that interest is just under 5.4% for ten-year loans, close to the highest level in 19 years.
The reason is that investors are worried. Prices in the UK are still rising quite fast, and they think the Bank of England might raise interest rates again to slow things down. Borrowing costs in America are also rising, which affects the UK too.
This matters for everyone. If the government spends more paying interest, it has less money for things like schools and hospitals. Banks also look at these rates when deciding how much to charge for mortgages.

levels.why: This makes it harder for the government to fund spending, and it can push mortgage rates up.

levels.body:
The UK government borrows a lot of money to pay for things like hospitals, schools and roads. It does this by selling something called gilts. People who buy them get paid interest.
At the moment, the government has to pay almost 5.4% interest on loans that last ten years. That's close to the most it has paid since 2007.
Lenders want more interest because they are worried. Prices in shops are still rising, and they think interest rates could go up again.
When the government pays more interest, there is less money left for public services. It can also make mortgages, the loans people use to buy homes, more expensive.

When the government spends more on interest, it has less to spend on things like schools, hospitals and roads.

headline: Bank of England holds rates at 3.75% but three members vote for a rise

levels.body:
The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee voted 6–3 to keep Bank Rate at 3.75% at its September meeting. Huw Pill, Catherine Mann and Megan Greene again voted for a 0.25-point rise to 4%.
The decision comes as higher global energy prices push inflation up again. CPI inflation rose to 3.1% in August, and the Bank expects it to reach around 3.75% in the final quarter of 2026 and slightly above 4% in early 2027, based on energy prices in mid-September.
Governor Andrew Bailey said higher energy costs had so far had a limited effect on UK prices and wages, but warned that the longer the volatility lasts, the more likely the Bank will need to raise rates. Domestic price pressures have continued to ease and the jobs market remains relatively soft.
levels.headline: Bank of England holds rates at 3.75% but three members vote for a rise
levels.why: A rate rise would make mortgages and loans more expensive for millions of households, and the three votes for a hike show it is a live possibility.

Governor Andrew Bailey said higher energy costs had so far had a limited effect on UK prices and wages, but warned that the longer the volatility lasts, the more likely a rate rise becomes. Inflation, the rate at which prices rise, went up to 3.1% in August, mostly because of higher global energy prices. The Bank now expects it to reach about 3.75% by the end of the year and slightly above 4% early in 2027.
Governor Andrew Bailey said energy costs had so far had only a limited effect on wider UK prices and wages. But he warned that the longer energy prices stay volatile, the more likely the Bank will need to raise rates to bring inflation back to its 2% target. The Bank of England has decided to keep interest rates at 3.75% for now. But three of the nine people who set rates wanted to raise them to 4%, which shows a rise could be coming.
The Bank is worried about inflation, which measures how fast prices are going up. It rose to 3.1% in August because energy and fuel have become more expensive around the world. The Bank expects it to go above 4% early next year.
The Bank's governor, Andrew Bailey, said that if energy prices stay high and unpredictable for a long time, the Bank will probably need to raise rates. Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive, which slows spending and helps bring prices down.

levels.why: If rates rise, mortgages and loans cost more.

levels.body:
The Bank of England sets the UK's main interest rate. This affects how much it costs people and businesses to borrow money, and how much savers earn.
This month, the Bank kept the rate at 3.75%. But three of the nine people who decide voted to raise it, so a rise could come soon.
The reason is that prices are rising faster again. Inflation reached 3.1% in August, mainly because fuel and energy cost more. The Bank thinks it could go above 4% early next year.
The Bank's boss, Andrew Bailey, said that if energy stays expensive for a long time, it will probably have to put rates up. That would make mortgages and loans cost more.

levels.why: Anyone with a mortgage or loan could end up paying more.

The Bank has decided to keep its rate at 3.75%. But some of the people who make the decision wanted to put it up.
They are worried because prices in shops are rising faster, mostly because fuel and energy are more expensive. Raising interest rates is one way to slow down rising prices, because people borrow and spend less.
If the rate goes up, families with mortgages, which are loans to buy a home, would have to pay more each month.

headline: UK inflation rises to 3.1% as fuel prices jump

levels.body:
UK CPI inflation rose to 3.1% in the 12 months to August, up from 2.9% in July and in line with forecasts. The rise was driven mainly by fuel: petrol rose 9.1p a litre between July and August and diesel 14.2p, leaving motor fuel prices 23% higher than a year earlier. Housing and household services, including domestic energy, also added to the rate.
Underlying measures were steadier. Core CPI held at 2.6% and services inflation was unchanged at 3.4%, while goods inflation rose from 2.2% to 2.7%.
The increase reflects global energy prices pushed up by the war involving Iran. Economists warn that continued volatility in oil and gas markets risks spreading into a wider range of goods and services.
levels.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.1% as fuel prices jump
levels.why: Higher fuel and energy costs squeeze household budgets and make a Bank of England rate rise more likely.

levels.body:
UK inflation rose to 3.1% in the year to August, up from 2.9% in July and in line with forecasts.
Fuel was the main driver. Petrol rose 9.1p a litre and diesel 14.2p in a single month, leaving motor fuel 23% more expensive than a year earlier. Household energy costs also contributed.
Underlying inflation was steadier. Core CPI, which excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, held at 2.6%, and services inflation stayed at 3.4%. Goods inflation rose from 2.2% to 2.7%.
The pressure comes from global energy markets disrupted by the war involving Iran, and economists warn that if it persists, higher costs could feed through to a wider range of goods and services.
levels.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.1% on fuel price jump
levels.why: Pricier fuel feeds into the cost of almost everything, and pushes the Bank of England towards higher rates.

levels.body:
Prices in the UK rose by 3.1% in the year to August, up from 2.9% in July. That figure, known as the inflation rate, was what economists expected.
The main reason was fuel. Petrol rose by 9.1p a litre and diesel by 14.2p in a single month, and fuel is now 23% more expensive than a year ago. Household energy bills also added to the rise.
Other prices are rising more steadily. Core inflation, which leaves out energy and food, stayed at 2.6%, and prices for services were unchanged at 3.4%. Goods prices rose faster, up from 2.2% to 2.7%.
Energy prices have climbed because of the war involving Iran. Economists warn that if oil and gas stay expensive, higher costs could spread to many other things people buy.
levels.headline: Fuel costs push UK inflation above 3%
levels.why: Drivers and households are paying noticeably more, and interest rates may rise as a result.

levels.body:
Prices in the UK are rising faster again. In August, things cost 3.1% more on average than a year earlier, up from 2.9% the month before.
The biggest reason is fuel. Filling up a car is now about 23% more expensive than a year ago. Diesel went up by more than 14p a litre in a single month. Home energy bills also rose.
If you leave out energy and food, prices are rising more slowly, at 2.6%. That suggests the problem is mainly about energy for now.
The war in the Middle East has pushed up the price of oil and gas. Experts worry that if it carries on, businesses will pass on higher costs, and more everyday things will get pricier.
levels.headline: Inflation climbs to 3.1% as petrol and diesel soar
levels.why: It makes everyday life more expensive, especially for people who drive.

levels.body:
Inflation is a measure of how quickly prices are going up. In August, prices in the UK were 3.1% higher than a year before. In July, the figure was 2.9%, so prices are now rising faster.
The main cause is fuel. Petrol and diesel have become much more expensive because of the war in the Middle East, which has pushed up the price of oil. Fuel now costs about 23% more than it did a year ago. Energy bills at home have gone up too.
When fuel costs more, it also costs more to transport food and other goods to shops. Experts worry this could make lots of other things more expensive too.
levels.headline: Fuel pushes UK inflation up to 3.1%
levels.why: Higher prices mean money doesn't stretch as far.

levels.body:
Prices in UK shops are going up faster than before. In August, things cost 3.1% more than they did a year earlier.
The biggest reason is petrol and diesel, the fuel used in cars, vans and lorries. It is now about a quarter more expensive than last year. That's because of a war in the Middle East, a region that produces a lot of the world's oil.
When fuel is expensive, it costs more to deliver food and other goods to shops. So prices of other things can start to rise too.
If prices rise faster than people's wages, families find that their money doesn't go as far as it used to.
levels.headline: Prices are rising faster, mainly because of fuel
levels.why: When prices rise faster than wages, people can afford less.

levels.body:
Things in UK shops are getting more expensive, and they are going up faster than before.
The main reason is petrol, the fuel that cars, buses and lorries use. Petrol and diesel cost a lot more than they did a year ago. That's because of a war far away, in a part of the world where lots of oil comes from. Petrol is made from oil.
Lorries use fuel to bring food and other things to the shops. When fuel costs more, the shops often have to charge more too.
This means families have to spend more money on the same things, so they have less left over for treats.
levels.headline: Petrol prices push up the cost of living
levels.why: Families have to spend more on the same things.

levels.body:
Things in the shops are getting more expensive. Grown-ups call this inflation.
The main reason is petrol. Petrol is what cars, buses and lorries use to drive. It is made from oil, and right now oil costs more because of a war in another part of the world.
Lorries carry food, clothes and toys to the shops. If petrol costs more, it costs more to drive the lorries. So the shops often have to make their prices higher too.
This means families need more money to buy the same things as before. That can make it harder to save up or buy treats.
levels.headline: Things cost more, mostly because of fuel
levels.why: Money doesn't go as far as it did.

levels.body:
Lots of things in the shops cost more than they used to.
One big reason is petrol. Cars, buses and lorries need petrol to go. At the moment, petrol costs a lot more because of a war in another part of the world.
Lorries bring food and toys to the shops. When petrol costs more, it costs more to drive the lorries. So the shops put their prices up.
That means families need more money to buy the same shopping. Grown-ups are hoping prices will stop going up so fast soon.
levels.headline: Petrol costs a lot more
levels.why: Families have less money left over.

levels.body:
Imagine your favourite snack costs 50p. Then one day you go to the shop and it costs 52p. Next time, it might cost even more.
That's what is happening to lots of things in the UK right now. Prices are going up.
One big reason is petrol. Petrol makes cars and lorries go. The lorries bring snacks and food to the shops. Petrol costs more now, because of a war far away.
So the shops have to charge a bit more. That means your pocket money buys a little less than it used to.
levels.headline: Things are getting pricier
levels.why: Money buys a little less.

headline: Oil heads for monthly gain of more than 8% as Hormuz talks stall

levels.body:
Brent crude rose back towards $98 a barrel on 30 September and was on course for a monthly gain of more than 8%, as uncertainty over US-Iran negotiations kept prices high.
Prices jumped more than 3% to above $107 on 28 September after President Donald Trump rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, saying Tehran's latest plan to end the US-Israeli war on Iran was not acceptable.
Before the war began in late February, about a fifth of the world's oil passed through the strait. Flows have partly recovered to 13.2 million barrels a day but remain below pre-war levels, keeping the market undersupplied.
levels.headline: Oil heads for monthly gain of more than 8% as Hormuz talks stall
levels.why: Oil prices feed directly into petrol, heating and transport costs, and are the main reason inflation is rising again in the UK and elsewhere.

levels.body:
Brent crude rose back towards $98 a barrel at the end of September, on course for a monthly gain of more than 8%.
Prices had jumped above $107 on 28 September after President Donald Trump rejected Iran's offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, calling Tehran's plan to end the war unacceptable.

levels.headline: Oil set for 8% monthly rise as Iran talks stall
levels.why: Expensive oil pushes up fuel and energy bills and drives inflation.

The price of Brent crude, the main global benchmark for oil, rose back towards $98 a barrel on 30 September and was on track to end the month more than 8% higher.
Prices jumped above $107 on 28 September after President Donald Trump rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days. He said Tehran's latest plan for ending the US-Israeli war on Iran was not acceptable.

Oil prices feed into petrol, heating and transport costs, and are a major reason inflation is rising in the UK.
levels.headline: Oil prices climb as US rejects Iran's offer
levels.why: Higher oil prices mean higher petrol and energy costs for households.

Oil prices rose more than 8% in September. A barrel of Brent crude, the price most of the world uses, was about $98 at the end of the month.
Prices spiked above $107 earlier in the week after President Donald Trump turned down Iran's offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within a week. Trump said Iran's plan for ending the war was not acceptable.
The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow stretch of sea next to Iran. Before the war started in February, about a fifth of the world's oil passed through it on tankers. More oil is getting through now than earlier in the war, but still less than normal.
When oil costs more, so do petrol, home heating and transport, which is pushing up prices in the UK.
levels.headline: Oil prices up 8% in a month
levels.why: It's a big reason petrol and energy bills are going up.

levels.body:
Oil is getting more expensive. The price of a barrel rose more than 8% in September, to about $98.
The main reason is the war between Iran on one side and the US and Israel on the other. Iran sits next to a narrow sea route called the Strait of Hormuz. Before the war, about one in five barrels of the world's oil travelled through it on ships. Since the fighting began, far fewer ships have got through.
Iran offered to reopen the route within a week, but President Donald Trump rejected its plan. Prices jumped above $107 when he did.
Oil is used to make petrol and to heat homes, so when oil costs more, those things do too.
levels.headline: Oil prices jump as US-Iran talks stall
levels.why: Fuel and energy bills follow oil prices.

levels.body:
Oil prices went up a lot in September, by more than 8%.

A lot of the world's oil normally travels on ships through a narrow stretch of sea next to Iran. But there is a war between Iran and the US and Israel, and fewer ships have been able to get through. Less oil reaching the rest of the world means it costs more.
Iran offered a plan to open the route again, but the US president said no. Until the war ends, oil prices are likely to stay high.
levels.headline: Oil is getting more expensive
levels.why: When oil costs more, so do petrol, heating and many other things.

Oil is getting more expensive. Oil is used to make petrol for cars and lorries. It is also used to heat homes and to make lots of things, like plastic.
Much of the world's oil comes from countries in the Middle East. It travels by ship through a narrow channel of sea. But there is a war in that area, so fewer ships are getting through.
When there is less oil to go around, people have to pay more for it. That's why oil prices went up a lot last month.
This is one of the main reasons petrol and energy bills are going up in the UK.
levels.headline: Oil costs more because of the war

Oil is a thick black liquid that comes from under the ground. It is used to make petrol for cars, and to make things like plastic toys.
Lots of oil is carried on big ships from one part of the world to the rest. The ships have to go through a narrow bit of sea.
Right now, there is a war near that narrow bit of sea, so fewer ships can get through. That means there is less oil for everyone.
When there is less of something that lots of people need, it costs more. So petrol costs more, and lots of other things cost more too.

People hope the war ends soon so the ships can sail safely again.

headline: Fed raises rates for the first time since 2023

levels.body:
The US Federal Reserve voted unanimously, 12 to 0, on 16 September to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 0.25 percentage points to 3.75%–4.00%. It was the Fed's first increase since 2023.
Chair Kevin Warsh said inflation had been too high for too long, with recent data still above the central bank's 2% long-run target.
In its statement, the Fed said economic activity was expanding at a solid pace. Domestic spending has been resilient, productivity growth is strong, business investment is robust, job gains have kept pace with the growth of the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.
Markets are pricing in one more quarter-point rise in 2026, followed by further increases into 2027.
Higher US rates tend to strengthen the dollar and push up borrowing costs worldwide, adding pressure on other central banks, including the Bank of England, which is weighing a rise of its own.
levels.headline: Fed raises rates for the first time since 2023
levels.why: Higher US rates lift borrowing costs worldwide and strengthen the dollar, adding pressure on other central banks, including the Bank of England.

levels.body:
The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate by 0.25 points on 16 September, to a target range of 3.75% to 4%. It was the first rise since 2023, and the decision was unanimous, 12 votes to none.
Chair Kevin Warsh said inflation had been too high for too long, with recent figures still running above the Fed's 2% target.
The Fed described the US economy as expanding at a solid pace, with resilient consumer spending, strong productivity, robust business investment and a broadly stable unemployment rate.
Markets expect one more quarter-point rise before the end of 2026 and further increases in 2027. Higher US rates tend to strengthen the dollar and lift borrowing costs around the world.
levels.headline: Fed hikes rates for the first time since 2023
levels.why: US rate rises ripple out to loans and markets around the world.

levels.body:
The US Federal Reserve raised interest rates on 16 September for the first time since 2023. All 12 voting members agreed to lift its main rate by a quarter of a percentage point, to a range of 3.75% to 4%.
The Fed's chair, Kevin Warsh, said inflation had been too high for too long. Recent figures show prices are still rising faster than the Fed's 2% target.
The Fed said the US economy is growing at a solid pace, with strong spending, investment and productivity, and that unemployment has changed little.
Investors now expect one more quarter-point rise before the end of 2026 and further increases in 2027. Because the dollar is so important to world trade, higher US interest rates tend to push up borrowing costs in other countries too.
levels.headline: US central bank raises interest rates
levels.why: When US rates go up, borrowing tends to get more expensive elsewhere too.

levels.body:
America's central bank, the Federal Reserve, has put its main interest rate up for the first time since 2023. It now sits between 3.75% and 4%.
All 12 voting members backed the rise. The Fed's chair, Kevin Warsh, said prices have been rising too fast for too long. The Fed aims to keep inflation at 2%, and it's been above that.
Raising interest rates makes borrowing more expensive, which encourages people and businesses to spend less. That should help slow down price rises.
Investors expect at least one more rise this year and more in 2027. Because the US is the world's biggest economy, its interest rates often affect borrowing costs in the UK and elsewhere.
levels.headline: Fed raises US rates to fight inflation
levels.why: It makes borrowing pricier in the US and can push up rates elsewhere.

levels.body:
The Federal Reserve, often called the Fed, is America's central bank. One of its jobs is to stop prices rising too quickly.
In September it raised interest rates for the first time since 2023, to between 3.75% and 4%. All 12 of the people who vote on it agreed.
The Fed's leader, Kevin Warsh, said prices in America have been rising too fast for too long. When interest rates go up, borrowing money costs more. People and businesses usually borrow and spend a bit less, which can help slow price rises.
Many experts think the Fed will raise rates again. What happens in America matters for the rest of the world, because so much global trade and borrowing is done in US dollars.
levels.headline: US interest rates go up for the first time since 2023
levels.why: Loans in the US get more expensive, with knock-on effects worldwide.

levels.body:
America has a central bank called the Federal Reserve. It decides how much it costs to borrow money in the US.
In September, it made borrowing more expensive for the first time in three years. It did this because prices in America have been rising too quickly.
The idea is that when borrowing costs more, people and companies spend less. When people spend less, shops can't put their prices up as easily, so prices rise more slowly.
People think the Fed may do this again soon. Because America is so big and powerful, this can also affect how much it costs to borrow money in the UK and other countries.
levels.headline: America's central bank puts interest rates up

headline: UK unemployment holds at 4.9% as job vacancies fall

levels.body:
The UK unemployment rate for people aged 16 and over was 4.9% in May to July 2026, the Office for National Statistics reported on 15 September. That is up 0.2 percentage points on a year earlier but largely unchanged on the previous quarter. In total, 1.78 million people were unemployed, 83,000 more than a year before.
Vacancies fell over the year to 702,000 in June to August, below pre-pandemic levels, suggesting employers are hiring more cautiously.
The economic inactivity rate, which counts people who are neither in work nor looking for it, fell 0.1 points to 20.9%.
Adjusted for inflation using the CPIH measure, regular pay grew 0.6% and total pay 0.9%, meaning wages are still rising slightly faster than prices.
A softening labour market is one of the reasons a majority of the Bank of England's rate-setters chose not to raise interest rates in September. The next figures are due on 20 October.
levels.headline: UK unemployment holds at 4.9% as job vacancies fall
levels.why: A softer jobs market means fewer openings and slower pay rises, and it is one reason the Bank of England is cautious about raising rates.

levels.body:
The UK unemployment rate was 4.9% in May to July, according to the Office for National Statistics, up 0.2 points on a year earlier but little changed on the previous quarter. That is 1.78 million people, 83,000 more than a year ago.
The number of job vacancies fell to 702,000 in June to August, below pre-pandemic levels, a sign that employers are hiring more cautiously.
The economic inactivity rate, the share of people neither working nor looking for work, dipped to 20.9%.
Pay is still beating inflation, but only narrowly: real regular pay rose 0.6% and real total pay 0.9%.
A softer jobs market is one reason the Bank of England is hesitant to raise rates. The next figures are due on 20 October.
levels.headline: UK unemployment steady at 4.9%, vacancies keep falling
levels.why: It is harder to find work than a year ago, and pay rises are only just keeping ahead of prices.

levels.body:
The UK's unemployment rate was 4.9% in the three months from May to July, according to the Office for National Statistics. That means about 1.78 million people who want a job don't have one, 83,000 more than a year ago.
Employers are also advertising fewer jobs. There were 702,000 vacancies between June and August, fewer than before the pandemic.
The share of people who are neither working nor looking for work, known as economic inactivity, fell slightly to 20.9%.
Wages are rising a little faster than prices. After taking inflation into account, regular pay grew by 0.6%. That's better than falling, but it's a small rise.
The next official figures will be published on 20 October.
levels.headline: Jobs market cools as vacancies drop below pre-pandemic levels
levels.why: Fewer vacancies make it tougher for young people and job seekers.

Finding a job in the UK has become a bit harder over the past year. Official figures show the unemployment rate is 4.9%, meaning about 1.78 million people want work but can't find it. That is 83,000 more than a year ago.
There are also fewer jobs on offer. Employers advertised 702,000 vacancies over the summer, fewer than before the pandemic.
Wages are still rising slightly faster than prices, but only by a small amount, around 0.6% for regular pay after inflation.
A weaker jobs market is one reason the Bank of England is being careful about raising interest rates, because higher rates could make things harder for employers and workers.
levels.headline: UK unemployment at 4.9%, with fewer jobs on offer
levels.why: Finding a job, especially a first job, is getting harder.

The unemployment rate shows the share of people who want a job but don't have one. In the UK it is now 4.9%. That is about 1.8 million people, and around 83,000 more than a year ago.

levels.headline: Unemployment steady at 4.9% as job adverts fall

levels.headline: Finding a job is getting a bit harder

headline: US 10-year Treasury yield touches 5.3%, highest since June 2007

levels.body:
The yield on the benchmark 10-year US Treasury note briefly touched 5.3% on Wednesday, its highest since June 2007. The 30-year yield reached 5.642%, a level last seen in June 2002. Yields move inversely to bond prices, so the rise reflects heavy selling of US government debt.
Equities closed a volatile September mixed. The S&P 500 fell 0.3% to 7,651.54 and the Dow also ended lower, while the Nasdaq Composite finished in positive territory. Thursday's open was modestly firmer: the S&P 500 up 0.20%, the Dow up 0.16% and the Nasdaq up 0.44%.
The data offered mixed signals. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index rose 0.3% in August, below the 0.4% consensus. But manufacturing expanded at a slower pace last month, and a gauge of raw-material prices rose to its highest since May, a possible sign of pipeline inflation.

The US government borrows by selling bonds called Treasuries. When investors sell those bonds, the interest rate, or yield, goes up. Investors are worried that inflation is not coming down and that the Federal Reserve will keep raising interest rates.
US shares had a bumpy end to September, with the S&P 500 falling 0.3%. There was some good news: an important measure of prices rose by 0.3% in August, a bit less than the 0.4% expected. But factory growth slowed, and the cost of raw materials rose to its highest since May.
Because so many loans around the world are linked to US rates, this can push up borrowing costs elsewhere.
levels.headline: US government borrowing costs hit highest level since 2007
levels.why: US government borrowing rates act as a benchmark for loans around the world, so a rise here tends to push up borrowing costs elsewhere.

levels.body:
The US government is paying more to borrow money than it has for 18 years. The interest rate on its ten-year loans briefly hit 5.3% on Wednesday, the highest since 2007.
Investors are demanding more because they are worried that prices in America are still rising too quickly, and that interest rates will keep going up.
Share prices on Wall Street were shaky at the end of September. A key measure of prices rose a little less than expected in August, which was welcome. But factories are growing more slowly, and the cost of the materials they use has risen.
Many interest rates around the world follow US rates, so this can make mortgages and business loans more expensive in other countries, including the UK.
levels.headline: US borrowing costs climb to an 18-year high
levels.why: When America's borrowing costs rise, mortgages and business loans tend to get more expensive, in the US and beyond.

levels.body:
Like the UK, the US government borrows huge amounts of money. It does this by selling bonds, a kind of IOU, to investors, who are paid interest in return.
This week, the interest on ten-year US bonds briefly reached 5.3%. That's the highest since 2007.
Investors want more interest because they are worried that prices in the US will keep rising and that interest rates will keep going up.
There was some good news: prices rose a bit less than expected in August. But factories are slowing down and the materials they need are getting more expensive.
What happens to US borrowing costs matters everywhere, because many other interest rates around the world follow them.
levels.headline: US borrowing costs hit an 18-year high
levels.why: When the US government pays more to borrow, loans tend to get dearer for everyone else too.

levels.body:
America borrows a lot of money. It does this by selling IOUs called bonds. People who buy them get paid interest.
Right now, people want more interest than they have for 18 years before they'll lend America money. That's because they are worried prices will keep going up and interest rates will stay high.
Prices in America rose a little less than people feared last month, which is good news. But American factories are slowing down.
When America has to pay more to borrow, other people often do too. That can make it more expensive to borrow money for a house or a business in lots of countries.
levels.headline: Borrowing money just got more expensive in the US
levels.why: Lots of other interest rates, like mortgages, follow US government borrowing costs, so this can make loans pricier around the world.

levels.body:
America is the richest country in the world, but it still borrows lots of money. When it borrows, it has to pay back a bit extra, called interest.
Right now, the extra America has to pay is the biggest it has been for 18 years. That's because the people lending the money are worried that prices will keep going up.
When America has to pay more to borrow, lots of other people often have to pay more too. That includes families borrowing money to buy a house, and companies borrowing money to grow.
So even though this is happening in America, it can affect people in the UK too.
levels.headline: The US is paying more to borrow money
levels.why: Other loans often follow this rate. So mortgages and business loans can get more expensive too.

levels.body:
America borrows a lot of money to pay for things. When you borrow money, you have to pay back a bit extra. That extra is called interest.
Right now, America has to pay back more extra than it has for a very long time. That's because the people lending the money are worried prices will keep going up.
When borrowing costs more for America, it often costs more for everyone else too, even in other countries.
That means families who borrow money to buy a home might have to pay more. That's why people are keeping an eye on it.
levels.headline: The US is paying more to borrow
levels.why: If borrowing costs more for the US, it usually costs more for everyone, including people getting a house loan.

levels.body:
America borrows lots of money. When it pays it back, it has to add a bit extra.
Right now, the extra is bigger than it has been for a very long time.
That's because the people lending the money are worried. They think things in shops will keep getting more expensive.
When America has to pay more extra, other people often have to pay more too, even in the UK.
So it could cost more for families to borrow money for things like a new house.
levels.headline: America has to pay more to borrow
levels.why: When borrowing costs more, people can't buy as many things.

Imagine you borrow a football from a friend. Your friend says, you can borrow it, but you have to give me a sweet when you give it back.
Now imagine your friend says, actually, you have to give me three sweets. Borrowing just got harder!
That's what is happening to America right now, but with money. America borrows lots of money, and now it has to give back more extra than it has for a very long time.
When borrowing gets harder for America, it often gets harder for other people too.
levels.headline: Borrowing costs a lot more in America
levels.why: When borrowing gets expensive, families and shops can afford to spend less.

headline: US avoids shutdown as new financial year begins

levels.body:
There was no US government shutdown on 1 October, the start of the federal 2027 financial year. A stopgap funding measure, known as a continuing resolution, was signed on 2 September and funds federal agencies generally at current levels through Friday 11 December.
Congress must pass appropriations bills each year to fund government departments. When funding lapses, non-essential operations stop and many federal employees are furloughed or work without pay until a deal is reached.
The House passed the short-term bill with enough votes to avoid a disruptive shutdown while lawmakers campaign for re-election in November's midterm elections, which will decide control of the House and Senate.
The measure postpones the harder negotiations over full-year spending until after polling day, setting up another deadline in December, during the lame-duck period before the new Congress takes office.
levels.headline: US avoids shutdown as new financial year begins
levels.why: It keeps public services and federal pay running for now, but sets up another funding showdown in December.

levels.body:
The US federal government did not shut down on 1 October, the start of its 2027 financial year. A stopgap funding bill, signed on 2 September, keeps federal agencies running at broadly current levels until Friday 11 December.
Under US law, Congress must pass spending bills each year. When it fails to, many agencies close and hundreds of thousands of federal workers are sent home or work without pay until a deal is done.
The House approved the short-term measure so that lawmakers could avoid a shutdown while campaigning for the November midterm elections, which will decide control of Congress.
The harder negotiations over full-year spending have been pushed past polling day, setting up another deadline in December.
levels.headline: No US shutdown as stopgap runs to 11 December
levels.why: Services stay open, but the funding fight returns in December.

levels.body:
The US government did not shut down on 1 October, the first day of its new financial year. Congress passed a short-term funding law, signed on 2 September, which keeps federal agencies running at broadly current levels until Friday 11 December.
In the US, Congress has to approve government spending every year. If it doesn't, many government departments have to close and some staff go unpaid, which is called a shutdown.
Lawmakers chose a temporary deal so they could avoid a messy shutdown while they campaign for re-election in November's midterm elections. The midterms decide who controls Congress for the next two years.
The fight over full spending plans for 2027 has been pushed back until after the election, so another deadline looms in December.
levels.headline: US government stays open thanks to short-term deal
levels.why: Federal workers keep getting paid, for now.

levels.body:
There's no US government shutdown this time. The new financial year started on 1 October, and Congress had already agreed a short-term law to keep government departments funded until 11 December.
In America, Congress must agree how much the government can spend each year. If it can't agree in time, parts of the government close down. Some workers are sent home, and some services stop. This is called a shutdown.
Many lawmakers are busy campaigning for the midterm elections in November and wanted to avoid a shutdown before voters go to the polls.
The temporary deal only delays the problem. Congress will have to agree a full budget, or another short-term deal, by 11 December.
levels.headline: No shutdown in Washington, for now
levels.why: Another deadline is coming at Christmas time.

levels.body:
In the US, Congress, which is America's parliament, has to agree how much money the government can spend each year. The new year for government spending starts on 1 October.
If Congress can't agree in time, some government offices close, some workers stop getting paid, and some services stop. This is called a shutdown.
This year, Congress agreed a temporary deal in September. It means the government stays open and keeps running as normal until 11 December.
Politicians wanted to avoid a shutdown before the midterm elections in November, when Americans vote for members of Congress. After the election, they'll have to sort out a longer deal.
levels.headline: US government funded until 11 December
levels.why: Services keep running, but the issue isn't settled.

levels.body:
In America, the government needs permission from Congress, America's lawmakers, to spend money. They have to agree a new budget every year, starting on 1 October.
If they can't agree, the government runs out of money. Some offices close and some workers don't get paid. This is called a shutdown.
This year, there was no shutdown. Congress agreed a short deal that pays for everything until 11 December.
There's a big election in America in November, and politicians didn't want a shutdown just before people vote. They'll have to agree a longer deal after the election.
levels.headline: The US government stays open
levels.why: People who work for the government keep getting paid.

levels.body:
In America, the government needs money to run things like national parks, passport offices and some airports. America's lawmakers have to agree how much it can spend every year.
If they can't agree in time, some government offices have to close. People who work there might not get paid. This is called a shutdown.
This year, the lawmakers agreed a short deal. That means everything stays open until December.
There's an election in America soon. Lawmakers didn't want things to close just before people vote. After the election, they'll have to agree again.
levels.headline: No US shutdown this time
levels.why: Government services keep working.

levels.body:
In America, the government runs lots of things, like national parks, museums and passport offices. All of these need money.
Every year, America's lawmakers have to agree how much money the government can spend. If they can't agree in time, some of these places have to close for a while. That's called a shutdown.
This year, they agreed to pay for things until December. So everything stays open for now.
They'll need to agree again before Christmas. If they don't, some places might close then.
levels.headline: America's government stays open
levels.why: Offices and services stay open.

In America, the government runs lots of places, like big parks and museums. These places need money to stay open.
Every year, America's leaders have to agree how much money to spend. If they don't agree, some places have to close.
This year, the leaders agreed to keep paying until December. So everything stays open for now.
They will have to agree again in December. People hope they will.
levels.headline: The government keeps going
levels.why: Things carry on as normal.

Imagine your family has a jar of money for paying for things like food and days out. Every year, the grown-ups have to agree how much to put in the jar.
If they can't agree, there's no money in the jar, and some things have to stop for a while.
America's leaders have a jar like that for the whole country. They had to agree by 1 October.
They did agree, but only until December. So everything carries on for now, and they'll talk about it again before Christmas.
levels.headline: Keeping the lights on
levels.why: Everything keeps working, for now.

headline: Conservatives gather in Birmingham for party conference

levels.body:
The 2026 Conservative Party Conference takes place from Sunday 4 to Wednesday 7 October at the ICC and Hyatt Regency in Birmingham. Since 2008, the event has alternated between Birmingham's International Convention Centre and Manchester Central.
Party conferences are held each autumn while the House of Commons is in recess. The four-day event combines main-hall speeches from senior figures, an exhibition and a large fringe programme of side events run by think tanks, campaign groups, charities and businesses. The focal point is the leader's speech on the final day.
The party, which lost power at the July 2024 general election, describes the conference as part of its renewal. It comes with Reform UK having led national opinion polls since early 2025, and in the same week as the Holborn and St Pancras by-election. The Conservatives will be under pressure to set out a clear offer and show how they plan to win back voters who have moved to Reform.
levels.headline: Conservatives gather in Birmingham for party conference
levels.why: Conference season is when parties set out their pitch to voters, and the Conservatives need to show how they will win back support from Reform.

Every autumn, the UK's big political parties each hold a conference. It's a few days where members, MPs and supporters get together to listen to speeches, discuss ideas and plan for the future.

headline: China's factories return to growth after two months of decline

levels.body:
China's official manufacturing purchasing managers' index rose to 50.1 in September from 49.8 in August, ending two months of contraction, National Bureau of Statistics data showed on Wednesday. The reading matched forecasts and came as Beijing announced stimulus to support the economy.
The improvement was led by equipment, high-tech and consumer industries. The production sub-index rose 1.3 points to 51.7 and new orders stood at 50.5. A private survey showed services growth at a three-month high of 51.6.
China's economy has been under pressure from weak domestic demand and investment and a struggling property sector, even as the global AI boom has lifted exports of high-tech goods.
levels.headline: China's factories return to growth after two months of decline
levels.why: As the world's biggest manufacturer, China's health affects global prices, trade and demand for raw materials.

levels.body:
China's official manufacturing PMI rose to 50.1 in September from 49.8 in August, returning to growth after two months of contraction. The reading matched forecasts.
Equipment, high-tech and consumer goods makers led the improvement. The production index climbed 1.3 points to 51.7 and new orders reached 50.5. A private survey showed services growing at a three-month high of 51.6.
The data comes as Beijing rolls out stimulus to support an economy weighed down by cautious consumers, weak investment and a struggling property sector. Exports of high-tech goods have held up, helped by the global AI boom.
As the world's largest manufacturer, China's factory health matters for global prices and demand for raw materials.
levels.headline: China's factories are growing again
levels.why: China's factories affect prices and trade around the world.

levels.body:
Activity in China's factories grew again in September after two months of decline. The official manufacturing index rose to 50.1, up from 49.8 in August. A score above 50 means activity is growing.
The rise came as the Chinese government announced measures to support the economy. Makers of equipment, high-tech goods and consumer products led the improvement. Production rose to 51.7 and new orders were 50.5. A separate survey showed China's services sector growing at its fastest pace in three months.
China's economy has been under pressure because people at home are spending cautiously, investment has been weak and the property market is struggling. At the same time, the global boom in artificial intelligence has boosted demand for Chinese high-tech exports.
levels.headline: Chinese factory activity picks up
levels.why: Much of what the world buys is made in China, so its factories matter to everyone.

levels.body:
China's factories got busier in September for the first time in three months. An official survey score rose to 50.1, just above the 50 mark that separates growth from decline.
The Chinese government has recently announced measures to help the economy, known as stimulus. Factories making equipment, high-tech goods and things for shoppers did best. Shops, restaurants and other services also grew at their fastest pace in three months.
China's economy has had problems. People there have been spending carefully, and the housing market has been weak. But demand for high-tech products, helped by the boom in artificial intelligence, has kept exports going.
Because China makes so much of what the world buys, its factories matter to prices everywhere.
levels.headline: China's factories start growing again
levels.why: A stronger China helps world trade.

levels.body:
Every month, China asks factory managers whether business is getting better or worse. The answers are turned into a score. Above 50 means factories are getting busier, below 50 means they are getting quieter.
In September, the score was 50.1. That means China's factories grew a little, after two months of shrinking.
The Chinese government has been trying to boost the economy, and that seems to be helping. Factories making machines and high-tech products did especially well.
China still has problems, including people spending less and a weak housing market. But this is a good sign. China makes a huge share of the world's goods, so what happens there affects prices and trade everywhere.
levels.headline: China's factories pick up

China still has some problems, like people there not spending much money. But busier factories are good news, for China and for the countries that buy what it makes.
levels.headline: China's factories are busier again
levels.why: China makes many of the things people buy around the world.

headline: US completes withdrawal of final troops from Iraq

levels.body:
The United States has withdrawn its last troops from Iraq, meeting the 30 September deadline set under a September 2024 agreement between Washington and Baghdad to wind down the US-led coalition against the Islamic State group. Iraq's prime minister had described the date as fixed and final.
About 2,500 US personnel had remained, training Iraqi forces and running counter-IS operations. Most bases elsewhere were vacated in 2025, with remaining forces consolidated in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region.
The exit ends the mission launched in 2014, when IS seized territory across Iraq and Syria, and a US military presence that began with the 2003 invasion to topple Saddam Hussein. It comes during the US-Israeli war on Iran, which has spilled into Iraq through clashes between US forces and Iran-backed militias, leaving Iraq's defence future uncertain.
levels.headline: US completes withdrawal of final troops from Iraq
levels.why: Iraq must now secure itself without US support while Iran-backed armed groups are active on its soil and a regional war continues next door.

levels.body:
The final US troops have left Iraq, meeting the 30 September deadline agreed with Baghdad in 2024. Around 2,500 personnel had remained, mostly in the Kurdish north, training Iraqi forces and carrying out operations against the Islamic State group.
The exit ends the counter-IS mission begun in 2014 and an American military presence that dates back to the 2003 invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein.
It comes at a volatile moment. The US-Israeli war on Iran has spilled into Iraq, with clashes between US forces and Iran-backed militias. With American troops gone, Iraq must now manage its own security while armed groups loyal to Tehran remain active inside the country.
levels.headline: Last US troops leave Iraq
levels.why: Iraq now has to manage its own security in a region at war, with Iran-backed groups active inside the country.

levels.body:
The last American troops have left Iraq, meeting the 30 September deadline agreed by the two governments in 2024. About 2,500 US personnel had remained, mostly in the Kurdish region in the north, training Iraq's forces and fighting the Islamic State group.
The US first invaded Iraq in 2003 to remove its leader, Saddam Hussein. Most troops left in 2011, but some returned in 2014 when Islamic State seized large areas of Iraq and Syria.
The pull-out happens during a war between Iran on one side and the US and Israel on the other. That conflict has spilled into Iraq, with clashes between US troops and armed groups backed by Iran. Iraq now has to manage its own security at a dangerous time.
levels.headline: US pulls its last soldiers out of Iraq
levels.why: Iraq is now responsible for its own security at a tense moment, with Iran-backed armed groups inside its borders.

levels.body:
The final American soldiers have left Iraq, on the deadline that both countries agreed in 2024. About 2,500 had stayed on, mainly in the north of the country.
American troops first went into Iraq in 2003, when the US invaded to overthrow its leader, Saddam Hussein. In recent years, they were there to train Iraq's army and help fight the Islamic State group, a violent extremist group that took over parts of Iraq and Syria in 2014.
The US has left while it is at war with Iran, Iraq's neighbour, together with Israel. Armed groups in Iraq that are backed by Iran have clashed with US forces. Iraq will now have to keep the country safe on its own.
levels.headline: Final US troops leave Iraq after 23 years
levels.why: Iraq now faces its security challenges alone while a war goes on next door.

levels.body:
American soldiers have been in Iraq, a country in the Middle East, since 2003. Now the last of them have gone home.
The US first went to war in Iraq to remove its leader at the time, Saddam Hussein. Later, American troops stayed to help Iraq fight a violent group called Islamic State, which took over parts of the country in 2014.
About 2,500 American soldiers were still there. They left on 30 September, the date the two countries had agreed.
It's a tense time. The US and Israel are at war with Iran, which is right next door to Iraq. Some armed groups inside Iraq support Iran. Iraq will now have to protect itself without American help.
levels.headline: US completes its pull-out from Iraq
levels.why: Iraq's security is now in its own hands at a dangerous moment for the region.

They first arrived in 2003, when America went to war to remove Iraq's leader. In recent years, they stayed to help Iraq's army fight a violent group called Islamic State.
The two countries agreed the soldiers would leave by 30 September, and they did.

levels.headline: American soldiers have left Iraq
levels.why: Iraq now has to protect itself, and some armed groups there are backed by Iran.

levels.body:
Iraq is a country in the Middle East. American soldiers have been there for 23 years. Now the last of them have gone home.
They first went to Iraq in 2003, during a war. Later, they stayed to help Iraq fight a dangerous group that had taken over some of its towns.
The two countries agreed the soldiers would leave by the end of September, and that's what happened.
Right now, there is a war near Iraq, between America and a country called Iran. So people are watching to see if Iraq can keep itself safe on its own.
levels.headline: The last US soldiers have left Iraq
levels.why: Iraq now has to keep itself safe without American help.

headline: Iran's rial falls to fresh record low beyond 2.5 million per dollar

levels.body:
Iran's currency, the rial, has fallen to a new record low of more than 2.5 million to the US dollar, less than a month after its previous record low.
The slide reflects the heavy toll the US-Israeli war on Iran, which began in late February, is taking on the country's economy. Iran was already under strain from years of international sanctions, high inflation and limited access to global markets. The war has added damage to infrastructure, disruption to oil exports and deep uncertainty about the future.
When confidence in a currency collapses, households and businesses rush to swap it for US dollars, gold or physical goods to protect their savings, which pushes the currency down further.
A weaker rial makes imported goods, including food, medicine, spare parts and fuel, far more expensive. Wages and savings lose value rapidly, eroding living standards for ordinary Iranians and increasing the risk of economic hardship and unrest.

headline: Kyiv braces for another winter of missiles, drones and blackouts

levels.body:
Kyiv, the capital of Ukraine, is preparing for another winter under Russian attack, with officials expecting missile and drone strikes and widespread power blackouts as temperatures fall.
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, each winter has brought sustained strikes on Ukraine's energy system, targeting power stations, substations, gas facilities and transmission lines. These attacks have repeatedly left millions of homes without heating, electricity and sometimes water, often for long periods in sub-zero temperatures.
Ukraine has strengthened its air defences and built physical protection around key energy sites, relying heavily on equipment and funding from allies in Europe and the United States. Repair crews and emergency generators are on standby to restore power as quickly as possible.
The risk is greatest for older people, people with health conditions and families with young children. Winter attacks on energy also increase pressure on Ukraine's allies to supply more air defence systems.

levels.why: Winter strikes on power and heating put civilians at serious risk and increase pressure on Ukraine's allies to supply air defence and help repair the grid.
